facts.text: In December 1804 the Dunbar–Hunter party camped on Calfait Creek, today Gulpha Creek.
In 1807 Jean Pierre Emanuel Prudhomme built the first real settlement at the springs and stayed two years.
Trapper John Percival built cabins to rent to the health seekers who came to the springs.
On Aug. 24, 1818, the Quapaw ceded the land around the hot springs to the United States.
The Belding family came from Massachusetts in 1828 and built a small hotel for visitors.
On April 20, 1832, President Andrew Jackson signed the act reserving the springs.
Hot Springs began in 1832 as a federal reservation, which the Encyclopedia of Arkansas calls the nation's first.
The 1832 Hot Springs Reservation is 40 years older than Yellowstone National Park.
The Rector family's claim to the springs rested on New Madrid Certificate No. 467, one of the title fights over the reservation.
facts.source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Rector v. United States

facts.text: Garland County was created in 1873, with Hot Springs as its seat.
The first Arlington Hotel opened in 1875.
Diamond Jo Reynolds's railroad carried visitors to Hot Springs from Malvern.
facts.source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Hot Springs Railroad

facts.text: In 1886 the Chicago White Stockings became the first major league club to hold spring training in Hot Springs.
An 1877 railroad booklet promoted Hot Springs by comparing it to the German spa Baden-Baden.
facts.source: NPS: Getting to the American Spa

facts.key: Ironing that set a curtain alight
facts.text: The Great Fire of Sept. 5, 1913, started with ironing that set a curtain alight.
After the 1913 fire, Hot Springs outlawed wood-shingle roofs.
The Buckstaff has offered baths continuously since 1912.
The Government Free Bathhouse gave about 87,040 free baths in 1919.
Carpenter Dam, completed in 1931, formed Lake Hamilton.
The Lamar's opening in 1923 completed Bathhouse Row.
During World War II an Army redistribution center in Hot Springs processed more than 32,000 service members.
In World War II the Army-Navy Hospital was the nation's largest center for adults with polio.
In 1946 the WWII veteran Sid McMath led the GI Revolt against the town's political machine.
The GI Revolt toppled the political machine of longtime Mayor Leo P. McLaughlin.
Blakely Mountain Dam creates Lake Ouachita, which flooded farm communities in the 1950s.
Keller and Marian Breland, a husband-and-wife team, opened the IQ Zoo in Hot Springs.
The IQ Zoo founders had trained under the psychologist B. F. Skinner.
In 1962 the Fordyce became the first Bathhouse Row bathhouse to close.
Passenger rail service to Hot Springs ended in 1964.
facts.source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Hot Springs Railroad

facts.text: The bathhouses were desegregated in 1965.
Gov. Winthrop Rockefeller ended the casino revival in 1967.
Bathhouse Row was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on Nov. 13, 1974.
By 1979 the Row gave about 96,000 baths a year, as bathhouses closed one by one.
In 1989 the Fordyce reopened as the park's visitor center.
The Superior, a 1916 bathhouse, now houses a brewery and distillery.
Quapaw Baths & Spa opened in the restored Quapaw Bathhouse in July 2008.
The Majestic Hotel caught fire on Feb. 27, 2014.
USGS says 47 hot springs emerge from Hot Springs Mountain.
Dating shows most of the thermal water is about 4,400 years old.
The bathing industry made Hot Springs known as the "Great American Spa."
The 1804 Dunbar–Hunter expedition measured the springs at about 148–150°F on average.

facts.key: There is no firm evidence he visited
facts.text: Legend says de Soto bathed here in 1541. Historians say there is no firm evidence he visited the springs.
Mountain Valley Spring Water, a Hot Springs bottled water, dates to 1871.
facts.source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Mountain Valley Spring Water

facts.text: Mountain Valley water comes out of its spring cold, not hot.
In 1920 a standard prescribed "course" was 21 baths.
Congress passed the act establishing the Government Free Bathhouse on Dec. 16, 1878.
The original Hot Springs Railroad from Malvern ran on 3 feet (narrow gauge) track.
facts.source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Hot Springs Railroad

facts.key: A guest traded it for an unpaid bill
facts.text: The McClard family got its famous barbecue sauce recipe when a guest traded it for an unpaid bill.
By 1928 the McClards were cooking goat with their barbecue sauce.
Campbell Arnoux was the founding director of KTHS radio, from 1924 to 1934.
facts.source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: KTHS Radio Station

facts.text: Lake Ouachita has about 200 islands.
Thermal water reaches the Superior Bathhouse Brewery at about 140°F.
facts.source: All About Beer: Superior Bathhouse Brewery

facts.text: The Maurice Bathhouse restoration, which broke ground in August 2025, is about $31.6 million.
facts.source: NPS: Groundbreaking celebrated for Maurice Bathhouse rehabilitation

facts.text: Each year teams race bathtubs down Central Avenue.
facts.source: Visit Hot Springs: 2020 version of the World Championship Running of the Tubs (press release)

facts.text: The Running of the Tubs began in 2006, per its organizers.
facts.source: Visit Hot Springs: Running of the Tubs 2026 press release

facts.text: The World's Shortest St. Patrick's Day Parade runs on Bridge Street.
facts.source: Visit Hot Springs: History of the shortest St. Patrick's parade

facts.text: Novaculite, the Ouachita whetstone rock, takes its name from the Latin for "razor stone."
Novaculite whetstone mining began in the Hot Springs region as early as 1818.
President Thomas Jefferson sent William Dunbar and George Hunter to explore the Ouachita country and its hot springs.
Dunbar and Hunter counted four principal springs and two lesser ones in 1804.
Native peoples quarried novaculite in the hills around Hot Springs for thousands of years.
Hot Springs was the capital of Arkansas from May 6 to July 14, 1862.
The Crystal Bathhouse, opened in 1904, was the first built exclusively for African Americans.
facts.source: NPS: African Americans and the Hot Springs Baths

facts.text: The Knights of Pythias opened the Pythian Bathhouse and Sanitarium in 1914.
facts.source: NPS: African Americans and the Hot Springs Baths

facts.text: The Army and Navy Hospital that opened in 1887 was the nation's first joint Army-Navy general hospital.
H. L. Campbell founded the alligator farm in 1902.
facts.source: Wikipedia: Arkansas Alligator Farm and Petting Zoo

facts.text: Lake Hamilton covers about 7,200 acres.
Remmel Dam, built in 1924, forms Lake Catherine.
The Civilian Conservation Corps built Lake Catherine State Park.
Lake Ouachita State Park preserves the historic Three Sisters Springs.
Verna Cook Garvan began developing Garvan Woodland Gardens in 1956.
Quartz crystal became Arkansas's state mineral in 1967.
facts.source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Official State Mineral

facts.text: The Hale is now the nine-suite Hotel Hale.
The Ozark Bathhouse now houses the Hot Springs NP Cultural Center.
Garvan Woodland Gardens on Lake Hamilton covers 210 acres.
The thermal spring water averages about 143°F.
The National Park Service says the springs produce over 700,000 gallons a day.
The white-to-tan rock around the spring openings is called tufa (travertine).
Two faults, the alpha and beta, help carry the heated water back to the surface.
The park's two cold springs, Happy Hollow and Whittington, are treated with ozone filtration.
The maple-leaf oak grows naturally at only four sites in the world, all in the Ouachitas.

contains: Absentee Shawnee Tribe, the Caddo Nation, the Osage Nation and the Quapaw Tribe

facts.text: People have lived here for over 10,000 years. The park has 92 known archaeological sites, including old novaculite quarries. The park consults with the Absentee Shawnee Tribe, the Caddo Nation, the Osage Nation and the Quapaw Tribe.
In 1860, 613 of Hot Spring County's 5,635 residents were enslaved, and many worked in the resort's hotels.
facts.source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Hot Springs (city) (via research/history-timeline.md)

contains: not during the 10 a.m.–noon hours doctors considered best

facts.text: In the 1880s Black bathers could buy tickets at a few bathhouses, but not during the 10 a.m.–noon hours doctors considered best. Bath attendants were mostly African American until the 1980s.
facts.source: NPS: African Americans and the Hot Springs Baths (via research/history-timeline.md)
